aliases: The Destruction of the First Temple

category: conquest, destruction of the Temple, and deportation
location: Jerusalem and the Kingdom of Judah; the deportees taken to Babylon

date.note: The Babylonian army under Nebuchadnezzar II took Jerusalem and burned the First Temple in 586 BCE (some reckonings give 587 BCE, depending on the chronology used for the regnal years in 2 Kings 25 and Jeremiah 52). The deportations occurred in stages: an earlier deportation is dated to 597 BCE (the exile of Jehoiachin, 2 Kings 24) and the main deportation to 586 BCE with the fall of the city. The return under Cyrus of Persia is conventionally dated to 538 BCE, following his conquest of Babylon in 539 BCE (Ezra 1). Years are given BCE; the negative 'year' field encodes 586 BCE.

summary: The Babylonian Exile is the Babylonian conquest of the Kingdom of Judah under Nebuchadnezzar II, the burning of the First Temple (Solomon's Temple) in Jerusalem in 586 BCE, and the deportation of much of the Judean elite to Babylon, ending the Kingdom of Judah. The biblical narrative records the siege and the destruction (2 Kings 25) and the exiles' lament by the rivers of Babylon (Psalm 137). The biblical writers read the catastrophe as the covenantal consequence of Judah's unfaithfulness, a reading attributed to those writers. The exile is conventionally held to have ended with the proclamation of Cyrus of Persia (538 BCE), after which returnees rebuilt the Temple, inaugurating the Second Temple period.
description:
The Babylonian Exile denotes the fall of the Kingdom of Judah to the Neo-Babylonian empire under Nebuchadnezzar II, the destruction of the First Temple, and the deportation of Judeans to Babylon in the early sixth century BCE. The biblical account in 2 Kings 25 relates that Nebuchadnezzar besieged Jerusalem, that in the fifth month Nebuzaradan, chief of the guards, came to the city and 'burned the House of GOD, the king's palace, and all the houses of Jerusalem' (2 Kings 25:9), that the Chaldean forces tore down the city walls, and that the remnant of the population was 'taken into exile by Nebuzaradan' (2 Kings 25:11). A first deportation had already occurred in 597 BCE with the surrender of the young king Jehoiachin (2 Kings 24); the destruction of the Temple and the main deportation followed in 586 BCE. These events ended the Davidic monarchy in Judah as an independent kingdom.

The experience of exile is given voice in Psalm 137, which opens 'By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat, sat and wept, as we thought of Zion' (Psalm 137:1) and vows 'If I forget you, O Jerusalem, let my right hand wither' (Psalm 137:5). The prophet Jeremiah, active before and during the fall of Jerusalem, is presented in the biblical books that bear his name as having foretold the Babylonian conquest and a seventy-year period of Babylonian domination, and as having counselled the exiles to settle in Babylon and seek its welfare (the biblical material at Jeremiah 25 and 29); the book of Ezra opens by dating the return to the fulfillment of 'the word of GOD spoken by Jeremiah' (Ezra 1:1). Within the biblical writings the destruction and exile are interpreted theologically, as the covenantal consequence of the people's and the kings' unfaithfulness to the covenant (brit) with the God of Israel, an interpretation that the present entry attributes to the biblical writers and the prophetic tradition rather than adjudicating as a historical cause of the events.

The exile is conventionally held to have ended after the Persian conquest of Babylon (539 BCE) with the proclamation of Cyrus of Persia, dated to 538 BCE, which the book of Ezra records as authorizing the return of exiles and the rebuilding of 'the House of the ETERNAL God of Israel' in Jerusalem (Ezra 1:2-3). The returnees and their descendants rebuilt the Temple, inaugurating what is called the Second Temple period. In the memory of the tradition the exile became a paradigm of loss, of continuity in dispersion, and of the hope of restoration, a hope later bound up with messianic expectation (mashiach). This entry records the conquest, the destruction of the Temple, the deportations, and the return as matters carried by the biblical text and by historical scholarship; it attributes the covenantal reading of the catastrophe to the biblical writers and does not adjudicate the theological interpretation as the historical cause.
editorial_notes:
This is one of the first two Event entries for the judaism tradition (Judaism previously had zero events); it is filed under data/events/judaism/ per ADR-0006 and ADR-0008. NEUTRALITY: the covenantal reading of the catastrophe (exile and the Temple's destruction as consequence of covenantal unfaithfulness) is a theological interpretation internal to the biblical writers and the prophetic tradition; per neutrality principles #1 and #2 it is ATTRIBUTED to those writers and NOT adjudicated by the editor as the historical cause of the Babylonian conquest, which is treated as a matter of Near Eastern political and military history. The dating (586 vs 587 BCE) is flagged in date.note as depending on the chronology used; the entry does not resolve it.

SOURCING triangulates three lenses per neutrality principles #8 and #9. (b) The OPEN PRIMARY corpus was read line-by-line at Sefaria and rated high only for the passages actually opened: 2 Kings 25 (the siege, the burning of the House of GOD at v.9, the deportation at v.11), Psalm 137 (the lament 'By the rivers of Babylon', vv.1 and 5), and Ezra 1 (the proclamation of Cyrus and the reference to the word of GOD spoken by Jeremiah, vv.1-3). The quoted wording follows the Revised JPS 2023 (Gender-Sensitive Edition) translation served by Sefaria; the underlying Hebrew is public domain and the URLs were confirmed to resolve. (a) The academic-history lens (Lester Grabbe, A History of the Jews and Judaism in the Second Temple Period) and (c) a contemporary Jewish scholar on the exile as a formative event (David Vanderhooft / Rainer Albertz-style treatment is represented here by Albertz, Israel in Exile) are rated medium: verified to exist and be on-topic via publisher and library records but not read line-by-line, so no high confidence is claimed for them. No encyclopedias, Wikipedia, or tertiary sources are cited.

Attributed to the biblical writers as their theological interpretation, not adjudicated by the editor as the historical cause of the Babylonian conquest.

In the memory of the tradition the loss of Temple and monarchy became bound up with the hope of restoration and, later, with messianic expectation (mashiach). Stated as a feature of the tradition's later reflection, not adjudicated.

The return under Cyrus (conventionally 538 BCE) and the rebuilding of the Temple inaugurated the Second Temple period; this entry links to second-temple-judaism as the era that follows the exile and the First Temple's destruction. Reported as a historical succession.
